plain.en: how much buyers are willing and able to buy at each price

means.en: fully
to order, to ask for
The amount of a good that buyers are willing to buy and able to pay for at each price. Wanting alone is not demand; the buyer must also have the money.

plain.en: what you can buy with the money you have

means.en: to buy
ability, strength
How much a buyer can actually buy with the money they have. Wanting something is not enough: a wish becomes demand only when the buyer can also pay the price.

plain.en: when a price rises, buyers take less of that good

means.en: a rule that holds again and again
how much buyers want and can pay for

The rule that price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, other things staying the same: at a higher price buyers take less, at a lower price they take more. This is why a demand curve slopes down from left to right.

plain.en: how much one buyer takes at each price

means.en: one single person
The demand of one buyer: how much that one person is willing and able to buy at each price. Srivalli's 1 kg at ₹150, 2 kg at ₹100 and 3 kg at ₹50 is her individual demand.

plain.en: a table of how much is bought at each price

means.en: how much buyers want and can pay for
a table of rows

A table that pairs each price with the quantity demanded at that price - the numbers before they are drawn. Srivalli's three rows are 1 kg at ₹150, 2 kg at ₹100 and 3 kg at ₹50; plotting those three rows is what draws the curve.

plain.en: a line on a graph showing how much a buyer takes at each price

means.en: how much buyers want and can pay for
a line drawn through plotted points

The line drawn by joining the points of a demand schedule, with price up the side and quantity along the bottom. It slopes down from left to right. When only the price changes, the buyer moves along the curve.

plain.en: how many of a good buyers take at one price

means.en: how much, how many
how much buyers want and can pay for
The amount buyers take at one given price, measured in kg here. It is one row of a demand schedule. It falls when the price rises and rises when the price falls.

plain.en: the total that all buyers want at each price

means.en: all the buyers and sellers together
how much buyers want and can pay for

The sum of the individual demand of every buyer at each price. At ₹100 per kg, Srivalli wants 2 kg, Alex 4 kg and Israt 6 kg, so the market demand is 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 kg. Like one buyer's curve, the market demand curve slopes down, but it is flatter.

plain.en: goods that can replace each other

means.en: under, in place of
stand

Two goods that do the same job for the buyer, so one can replace the other, like tea and coffee. If coffee becomes costlier while the price of tea stays the same, some people switch to tea, so the demand for tea rises.

plain.en: goods that are used together

means.en: together
fill

Two goods that are used together, like cars and petrol, or movie tickets and cinema popcorn. If movie tickets become costlier, fewer people go to the cinema, so the demand for popcorn falls, even though its own price has not changed.

plain.en: each extra one gives less extra satisfaction

means.en: grow less
of one extra unit
usefulness, how much it is wanted

Each extra unit of a good gives less extra satisfaction than the one before. The first mango tastes delicious, the second is good, and by the third you hardly want it. So a buyer is willing to pay less for each extra mango. This is one reason people buy more only at a lower price.

plain.en: how much sellers are willing and able to offer at each price

means.en: from below, up
to fill
The amount of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at each price. Willing means the price is worth it to them; able means they really have the goods.

plain.en: when a price rises, sellers offer more

means.en: a rule that holds again and again
how much sellers offer for sale

The rule that price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, other things staying the same: at a higher price sellers offer more, at a lower price they offer less. This is why a supply curve slopes up from left to right.

plain.en: how much one seller offers at each price

means.en: one single person
how much sellers offer for sale
The supply of one seller: how much that one seller is willing and able to offer at each price. Seller A's 1 kg at ₹50, 2 kg at ₹100 and 3 kg at ₹150 is his individual supply.

plain.en: how many of a good sellers offer at one price

means.en: how much, how many
how much sellers offer for sale
The amount sellers offer at one given price, measured in kg here. It is one row of a supply schedule. It rises when the price rises and falls when the price falls.

plain.en: the total that all sellers offer at each price

means.en: all the buyers and sellers together
how much sellers offer for sale

The sum of the supply of every seller at each price. At ₹100 per kg, Seller A offers 2 kg, Seller B 4 kg and Seller C 6 kg, so the market supply is 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 kg. Like one seller's curve, the market supply curve slopes up, but it is flatter.

plain.en: a line on a graph showing how much a seller offers at each price

means.en: how much sellers offer for sale
a line drawn through plotted points

The line drawn by joining the points of a supply schedule, with price up the side and quantity along the bottom. It slopes up from left to right. When only the price changes, the seller moves along the curve.

plain.en: the price at which buyers want exactly what sellers offer

means.en: all the buyers and sellers together
equal
balance

The point where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied, so there is neither a surplus nor a shortage. In the mango market it is at ₹100 per kg and 12 kg. In real markets demand and supply keep changing, so the equilibrium keeps moving.

plain.en: more offered than buyers want, at that price

means.en: over, beyond
more

Excess supply: at a price, sellers offer more than buyers want, so some goods are left unsold. At ₹150 the mango market has 18 kg offered and 6 kg wanted, a surplus of 12 kg. A surplus pushes the price down.

plain.en: more wanted than sellers offer, at that price

means.en: not enough

Excess demand: at a price, buyers want more than sellers offer, so some buyers go without. At ₹50 the mango market has 18 kg wanted and 6 kg offered, a shortage of 12 kg. A shortage pushes the price up.

plain.en: the price a hotel charges for a room

means.en: The price charged for a service, such as a hotel room for one night. A hotel in Goa may charge ₹1,500 on a Monday in July and ₹25,000 on New Year's Eve. The same word is also used for a tax on goods brought in from another country.

plain.en: all the money a business earns from its sales

means.en: back
to come
The total amount of money a business earns from selling goods or services, before any costs are taken out. A hotel changes its tariff to earn the most revenue from its rooms.

plain.en: a market with only one seller

means.en: one, single
seller

A market where one seller controls the whole supply of a product that has no close substitute. With no other seller to compete with, it can charge a higher price and supply less. The government keeps such sellers in check.

plain.en: the highest price a seller is allowed to charge

means.en: what a thing costs
a cap, the top allowed

A highest price set by the government, for example on medicines. It changes things only when it is below the market price. Then buyers want more than sellers offer, so there is a shortage. In the mango market, a ceiling of ₹50 per kg would leave a shortage of 12 kg.

plain.en: the lowest price that may be charged

means.en: what a thing costs
a base, the lowest allowed

A lowest price set by the government. It changes things only when it is above the market price. A minimum wage is a price floor: an employer must pay at least that wage, so that workers earn enough for their work.

plain.en: keeping far more goods than you need, often hidden

means.en: a hidden store
Keeping far more goods, or money, than is needed now, usually out of fear of a shortage or in the hope of selling later at a higher price. In 2020 some shopkeepers hoarded sanitisers.

plain.en: selling goods secretly against the rules

means.en: secret, against the law
buying and selling
Buying and selling goods or services that are banned or controlled, in secret, for example selling sanitisers above the allowed price in 2020.

plain.en: goods and services that everyone can use, such as roads and parks

means.en: of all the people
things people use

Goods and services provided by the government for everyone, such as roads, bridges, parks, streetlights, defence and drainage. Private companies usually do not provide them, because they earn no direct profit from them.

plain.en: how simple it is to start, run and close a business

means.en: with little trouble
How simple it is to start, run and close a business in a country. Many permissions, long waits and costly paperwork make it harder, most of all for small businesses.
